name: Charles G. Finney

born.place: Warren, Litchfield County, Connecticut, United States

life_summary: Charles Grandison Finney was born in Warren, Connecticut, in 1792. He grew up in Oneida and Jefferson counties in upstate New York, taught school in New York and New Jersey, and from 1818 worked in Benjamin Wright's law office at Adams, New York. After a conversion experience at Adams on 10 October 1821 he left law, was licensed to preach by the St. Lawrence Presbytery in December 1823, was ordained in 1824, and married Lydia Root Andrews that October. From 1824 to 1832 he led revival campaigns in upstate New York and in Philadelphia, New York City, Rochester and Boston, and ministers opposed to his "new measures" debated them with him at New Lebanon in July 1827. He then led New York City congregations at Chatham Street Chapel (1832–36) and the Broadway Tabernacle (1836–37), published Lectures on Revivals of Religion in 1835, and in 1836 left the Presbytery to identify as a Congregationalist. He became professor of theology at Oberlin, Ohio, in 1835, settled there in 1837, was pastor of its First Congregational Church until 1872, served as president of the college from 1851 until he resigned in 1865 (some sources say 1866), and made preaching tours of Britain in 1849–51 and 1858–60. Widowed in 1847 and 1863 and married three times, he taught until July 1875, died at Oberlin on 16 August 1875, and his Memoirs were published in 1876.

phases.label: Youth and schoolteaching
phases.summary: Born in Warren, Connecticut, he grew up in Hanover (Oneida County), New York, attended Oneida Academy, and taught district school at Henderson from 1808 to 1812. After a stay in Warren, Connecticut, he taught school in New Jersey from 1814, returning to Henderson, Jefferson County, New York, in 1818.
phases.place: Warren, Connecticut; Hanover and Henderson, New York; New Jersey

phases.label: Itinerant revivalist campaigns
phases.summary: Ordained in 1824 and newly married, he worked as a missionary in Jefferson County and then led revivals in Oneida County (1826–27), Delaware and Pennsylvania (1827–29), New York City (1829–30), Rochester (1830–31) and Boston (1831–32). His children Helen (1828), Charles (1830) and Frederic (1832) were born in these years.
phases.place: Jefferson and Oneida counties, NY; Philadelphia; New York City; Rochester; Boston

phases.label: New York City pastorates
phases.summary: He was pastor of the Second Free Presbyterian Church at Chatham Street Chapel (1832–36) and then of the Broadway Tabernacle (1836–37); cholera in 1832 and a Mediterranean voyage for his health in 1834 interrupted this work. From 1835 he also held the professorship of theology at Oberlin, and his daughter Julia was born in March 1837.
phases.place: New York City; Oberlin, Ohio (professorship from 1835)

phases.label: Oberlin pastor and professor
phases.summary: Settled at Oberlin as pastor of the First Congregational Church and professor of theology, he also preached revivals in Rochester, Boston and Providence (1842) and published Lectures on Systematic Theology (1846–47). His daughter Sarah died in 1843 and his wife Lydia in 1847; he remarried in 1848 and preached in England from November 1849 to 1851.
phases.place: Oberlin, Ohio; also Rochester, Boston, Providence and England

phases.label: Oberlin College presidency
phases.summary: As president of Oberlin College he kept his pastorate and teaching, and made a second preaching tour of England and Scotland (1858–60). His daughter Delia died in 1852 and his second wife Elizabeth in 1863.
phases.place: Oberlin, Ohio; also England and Scotland

phases.label: Final years at Oberlin
phases.summary: After resigning the presidency and marrying Rebecca Allen Rayl in 1865, he stayed on as pastor of the First Congregational Church until 1872, published a book against Freemasonry (1869), began writing his Memoirs (1867), and taught pastoral theology until July 1875. He died at Oberlin in August 1875.
